extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and students of political sociology/history of science (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the 'militant' type of society by the traits and institutional features Spencer lists; also includes historical methods for measuring Earth's mean density described earlier in the same issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountain-attraction (deflection of a plumb-line) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure deflection of a plumb-line near a mountain and deduce relative masses / densities from the law of attraction (as done by Maskelyne and Hutton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires estimating the mountain's mass, mean density, and center-of-gravity distance from the lead; calculations follow from gravitational proportion. Results are liable to error because the mountain elements were estimated rather than accurately measured; great exactness cannot be claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendulum method for earth's density
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare durations of pendulum oscillations at different elevations to calculate the amount of gravity and hence mean density of the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes the local surface is plane and part of an exact sphere; oscillations of the same pendulum considered equal if departure from vertical ≤ 5°. Nearby mountains distort local gravity and make oscillations more rapid, so difference between calculated and observed rates indicates mountain influence. Subject to same defects as mountain method because mountain elements used in corrections are often estimated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torsion-balance (Cavendish-style) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a torsion balance with known masses and measured deflections to compute the force of attraction between masses and thence the ratio of earth mass to known masses, yielding mean density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instrument: a rod with suspended balls, movable lead balls brought close to produce minute horizontal deflections measured via a mirror and graduated circle. Since masses, relative distances, and absolute weights are measurable, this method gives clear determinations with only small possible errors; historically considered highly trustworthy (Cavendish, Reich, Baily results cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-armed balance (Jolly/Poynting) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach a weight to a long rod and oppose a counter-weight; bring a test ball under the weight to produce a tiny disturbance of the balance from which attraction is computed to infer mean density of the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires precise weights, carefully measured center-to-center distances, and highly sensitive detection of tiny balance disturbances (example: disturbance of 0.01 mg). Poynting calculated mean density as 5.69 with probable error ±0.15, illustrating the need for careful measurement and instrument sensitiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-method agreement as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate agreement among results from multiple independent methods justifies confidence that interior masses of the earth possess high density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare values from different measurement approaches (mountain-deflection, pendulum, torsion-balance, two-armed balance); where values roughly converge, one may infer robust conclusions (e.g., internal parts must have metallic constitution given crust densities vs mean density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete corporate action (militant societies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A militant society is one in which for preserving corporate life all capable members combine their actions in concert for offence and defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic: the fighting body tends to include all men fit for bearing arms and trusted with arms; universal militant cooperation improves probability of survival in inter-societal struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-combatant permanent commissariat
rubrics_metrics.description: In purely militant societies, non-combatants (women, enslaved captives, serfs) must devote their lives to supporting and maintaining the combatant class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-combatants' labor is subordinated to the needs of fighters; societies where non-combatants retain more produce weaken the fighters' exclusive support and thus fighting capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximized warrior-to-worker ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: The militant tendency is for the body of warriors to bear the largest practicable ratio to the body of workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A non-combatant class should not expand beyond what efficiently fulfills its supporting purpose; otherwise fighters are undersupported or too few relative to workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding together / centralized cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Militant societies develop close binding and strong bonds so units act as a single, efficient fighting structure (solid phalanx vs loose group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cohesion ensures prompt combined action; loose groups are disadvantaged in warfare compared to tightly bound societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of the individual (life, liberty, property)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the militant type the individual's life, liberty, and property are subordinated to the society; life is at the disposal of the state, freedom is limited to what military obligations allow, and property may be surrendered for public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual rights are secondary to preservation of the society; private ownership may exist by permission only and be overridden when the public requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coercive instrumentality and tendency toward despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete corporate action presupposes a coercive controlling agency; chronic militancy tends to develop despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because division of counsel is fatal in war, societies favor powerful central control that enforces unity; despotism and strong centralized control are adaptive under persistent militancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization and graded hierarchy (status-based organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Militant societies are characterized by centralized administration with successive grades of subordination (commander-in-chief, secondary commanders, etc.), extending status relations through civil and military life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulative structure mirrors military grades; workers and fighters alike come under hierarchical control, producing a society of status where each person is master of those below and subject to those above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regimentation extending beyond the army
rubrics_metrics.description: Regimentation begun in the military spreads to civil society, producing widespread supervision and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily civilian life becomes similar to military life where occupation differs; labor is carried on under coercive control and supervision spreads everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive and negative regulation by government
rubrics_metrics.description: A militant government not only restrains (negative regulation) but prescribes and enforces actions (positive regulation) — telling individuals what to do as well as what not to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive regulations can be detailed and peremptory, making civilian conduct resemble soldierly obedience to orders; compulsory cooperation is the fundamental principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory cooperation as the core principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The militant type is fundamentally based on compulsory cooperation: members are forced to act together for defence/offence and non-combatants are compelled to support them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compulsory cooperation secures military efficiency but restricts voluntary action and individual autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixity of status, inheritance, and occupational rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Militant organization fosters transmission of ranks and occupations by inheritance, resisting upward mobility and fixing special functions across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superiors have an interest in replacing workers with capable successors, and workers have incentives to train sons in same occupations; over time this produces social rigidity and entailed restraints on movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on movement and need for locational knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals in a militant society are often tied to localities and must be constantly locatable (soldier at hand, slave cannot leave allotment, serf bound to land).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such restraints ensure the permanent base of operations (non-combatant support) remains available to combatants; mobility is discouraged in proportion to subordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression or regulation of private associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations outside the state (commercial bodies, religious societies, philanthropic groups) are absent, rare, or officially regulated in the militant type because independent associations limit centralized administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If private combinations are allowed, they are constrained by official regulation which prevents independent action and improvement; voluntary cooperation institutions are incongruous with compulsory-cooperation societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toleration of private combinations only if military-like
rubrics_metrics.description: Private combinations that survive in militant societies are those congruous with the militant principle (factions, primitive guilds for mutual protection, secret societies) and are themselves coercive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These smaller societies replicate ends of the larger society on a smaller scale and are organized by compulsory cooperation, sometimes enforcing obedience severely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic autonomy and self-sufficiency (protectionist tendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A militant society tends toward internal provision of necessary supplies and economic self-sufficiency to avoid dependence on potentially hostile neighbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent hostilities hinder external commerce, so groups strive to produce most articles internally; this yields a protectionist policy and structures to maintain internal production (e.g., feudal castles producing many needed goods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire not to be dependent on foreigners
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideological/economic trait: militant societies value not being dependent on foreigners for supplies and thus favor domestic production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This desire follows from strategic necessity: if supplies from other countries may be cut off by hostilities, internal capacity must be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Manifestations of militant traits can be observed in small primitive groups (female labour as commissariat, enslavement, temporary chiefs becoming permanent) and in highly militant states (e.g., Dahomey: absolute king, sumptuary laws, extreme regimentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ethnographic and historical examples to test presence of militant traits: coextensive fighting body, subordinated private claims during war, emergence of despotism, sumptuary laws, and extreme regimentation are evidence.
